ai.literal: To fatten one's own flesh, oneself another's flesh eats, how will possess compassion?
ai.translation: How can he possess compassion, who eats the flesh of another living being to fatten his own flesh?
ai.modern: தன் உடம்பின் சதையை வளர்ப்பதற்காக, மற்றொரு உயிரினத்தின் உடம்பின் சதையை உண்பவன் எவ்வாறு அருளைப் பெற முடியும்?
ai.explanation: This couplet opens the chapter on abstaining from flesh-eating by questioning the compatibility of meat-eating with compassion. The poet contrasts 'one's own flesh' (தன் ஊன்) with 'another's flesh' (பிறிது ஊன்). To grow one's own body by consuming the body of another sentient being is presented as a fundamental contradiction to the concept of 'aruḷ' (compassion or grace). The rhetorical question 'how will he possess compassion?' emphasizes that true mercy cannot coexist with the act of killing and eating other living creatures for personal nourishment.

words.gloss: to those who do not protect

ai.literal: The possession of wealth does not exist for those who do not protect it; likewise, the possession of grace does not exist for those who eat flesh.
ai.translation: Just as the possession of wealth is impossible for those who do not guard it, the possession of grace is impossible for those who eat meat.
ai.modern: செல்வத்தைப் பாதுகாத்து ஆளாதவர்களுக்குச் செல்வத்தின் பயன் இல்லை; அதுபோல, பிற உயிர்களின் ஊனைத் தின்பவர்களுக்கு அருளின் ஆட்சி இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a clear analogy to show that compassion cannot coexist with meat-eating. Just as those who do not guard and manage their material wealth (poruḷāṭci) cannot enjoy its benefits, those who consume the flesh of other living beings (ūṉtiṉpavar) cannot possess the reign of grace or compassion (aruḷāṭci). The poet emphasizes that compassion is a treasure that must be actively nurtured, and eating meat is fundamentally incompatible with it.

ai.literal: Like the heart of those who hold weapons, the mind of those who ate the taste of another's body does not harbor goodness.
ai.translation: Like the heart of those who hold weapons of slaughter, the mind of those who feast on the flesh of another creature cannot harbor compassion.
ai.modern: ஆயுதம் ஏந்திய கொலைஞர்களின் நெஞ்சத்தைப் போல, பிறிதொரு உயிரின் உடலைச் சுவைத்து உண்டவர்களின் மனம் நன்மையை (அருளை) நாடாது.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares the mind of a meat-eater to that of a weapon-wielding killer. The word 'படைகொண்டார்' refers to those who hold weapons of slaughter, whose hearts are hardened to the pain of living beings. The poet states that the mind of someone who relishes the taste of another creature's body ('ஒன்றன் உடல்சுவை உண்டார்') is similarly incapable of harboring true goodness or compassion ('நன்னூக்காது'). Eating flesh requires ignoring the suffering of the animal, which naturally deadens the capacity for mercy.

ai.literal: If you ask what is grace, it is non-killing; killing is the lack of virtue, and eating that flesh is also not a virtuous thing.
ai.translation: If you ask what compassion is, it is the practice of non-killing; killing is the absence of compassion, and eating that flesh is devoid of any virtue.
ai.modern: அருள் என்பது எது என்றால் அது கொல்லாமை ஆகும்; உயிரைக் கொல்லுதல் அருள் இல்லாத தன்மை ஆகும்; அந்த உடலை (ஊனை) உண்பதும் அறம் அல்லாதது ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the essence of compassion as the practice of non-killing. It explains that if one asks what compassion is, the answer is simply not taking any life. Conversely, killing is the very opposite of compassion, and consuming the meat of a killed creature is completely devoid of virtue. The poet emphasizes that one cannot claim to have compassion while participating in the consumption of meat obtained through killing.

words.gloss: opening the mouth to let escape

ai.literal: Abstaining from eating flesh is that which sustains the maintenance of life; if one eats flesh, hell will not do opening of its mouth to let them escape.
ai.translation: The preservation of life is sustained by abstaining from eating flesh; if one eats flesh, hell will swallow them and never open its mouth to let them escape.
ai.modern: புலால் உண்ணாமல் இருப்பதே உயிர்கள் நிலைபெற்று வாழ்வதற்குக் காரணமாகும்; ஒருவன் புலால் உண்டால், நரகம் அவனை விழுங்கிவிட்டு மீண்டும் வெளியேற வழிவிடாது.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the spiritual and moral consequences of eating meat. The first part states that the preservation of life is rooted in abstaining from eating flesh. The second part warns that if a person eats meat, hell will swallow them and will not open its mouth to let them escape. The word 'aṇṇāttal' refers to opening the mouth or looking up, suggesting that hell holds the meat-eater so tightly that there is no hope of rising or escaping from its depths.

ai.literal: If the world does not kill for the sake of eating, no one will give meat for the sake of price.
ai.translation: If the world does not slaughter animals for the sake of eating, no one will offer meat for sale.
ai.modern: உலக மக்கள் சாப்பிடுவதற்காகக் கொலை செய்ய மாட்டார்கள் என்றால், விலைப் பொருளுக்காக இறைச்சி விற்பவர் யாரும் இருக்க மாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the direct link between demand and supply in the meat trade. It argues that the slaughter of animals happens only because people want to consume meat. If the public refrains from eating meat for their food, the commercial incentive to kill animals for profit will cease to exist. Thus, those who consume meat share the responsibility for the killing alongside those who sell it.

ai.literal: Abstaining from eating is required of flesh, which is the wound of another one, if those who understand this are found.
ai.translation: One must abstain from eating flesh, if one realizes that meat is nothing but the raw wound of another living being.
ai.modern: புலால் என்பது வேறொரு உயிரினுடைய உடலின் புண் என்பதை மக்கள் உணர்ந்தால், அதை உண்ணாமல் தவிர்க்க வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet presents a powerful argument for vegetarianism by redefining what meat actually is. The poet uses the word 'puṇ' (புண்), meaning a wound or sore, to describe flesh. By realizing that meat is not just food but the mutilated, wounded body of another living creature, a person of understanding will naturally feel aversion. The couplet suggests that abstaining from meat is a logical consequence of truly perceiving the pain and suffering inherent in its origin.

ai.literal: From delusion completely separated vision-possessors will not eat from life completely separated flesh.
ai.translation: Those with clear vision, completely freed from delusion, will not eat flesh that has been completely severed from life.
ai.modern: குற்றமற்ற தெளிந்த அறிவுடையவர்கள், உயிரிலிருந்து பிரிந்துபோன உடலாகிய இறைச்சியை உண்ணமாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains that eating meat is incompatible with true wisdom and clarity of mind. The poet describes wise people as those who have completely freed themselves from the blemish of delusion. Such individuals of clear vision will never consume meat, which is defined here simply as substance completely severed from a living being. By showing that a clear mind naturally rejects meat, the verse highlights the connection between mental clarity and compassion toward all life.

ai.literal: Than performing a thousand sacrifices by pouring offerings, not eating [flesh] by destroying the life of a single being is better.
ai.translation: Abstaining from killing even a single living being and eating its flesh is far better than performing a thousand sacrifices by pouring rich offerings into the fire.
ai.modern: அவிப்பொருள்களைச் சொரிந்து ஆயிரம் வேள்விகளைச் செய்வதை விட, ஓர் உயிரைக் கொன்று அதன் உடலை உண்ணாமல் இருப்பது மிகவும் நல்லது.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares ritual piety with ethical compassion. The author states that performing a thousand elaborate fire sacrifices (வேட்டல்) with rich offerings (அவி) is of lesser value than the simple act of refraining from killing a single living being (உயிர் செகுத்து) and eating its flesh (உண்ணாமை). The word 'அவி' refers to the sacred offerings like ghee or grains poured into the sacrificial fire, while 'செகுத்து' means destroying or killing. By placing the preservation of a single life above a thousand grand religious rituals, the couplet emphasizes that non-killing and compassion are the highest virtues.

ai.literal: Him who does not kill and who abstained from flesh, with folded hands, all living beings will worship.
ai.translation: All living beings will fold their hands and worship the one who does not kill and who abstains from eating flesh.
ai.modern: ஓர் உயிரையும் கொல்லாதவனாகவும், புலால் உண்பதைத் தவிர்த்தவனாகவும் இருப்பவனை, உலகிலுள்ள எல்லா உயிர்களும் கைகூப்பி வணங்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme spiritual status of a person who practices absolute non-violence. By refusing to kill any creature (கொல்லான்) and refusing to consume meat (புலாலை மறுத்தான்), a person rises above the cycle of harm. Such an individual radiates peace and harmlessness so profoundly that all living creatures (எல்லா உயிரும்), losing their natural fear, will revere them with folded hands (கைகூப்பி தொழும்). It shows that true greatness lies in universal compassion.
